area: Area IV. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how air, weight and wind change your takeoff, fly a normal and a crosswind takeoff step by step, hold VY +10/-5 knots, and plan for a rejected takeoff or an engine failure.
why: About one in five general aviation accidents happen during takeoff and departure climb, and more than half of those are pilot failures, many from loss of control [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

prereading.what: Normal takeoff, crosswind takeoff, common errors, ground effect, VX and VY.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 6, 6-1 to 6-10

prereading.what: Rejected takeoff, engine failure on climb-out, noise abatement.
prereading.label: AFH 6-14

prereading.what: Runway surface and slope, takeoff performance, effect of weight, wind and density altitude.
prereading.label: PHAK 11-12 to 11-16

prereading.what: Engine failure after takeoff and why turning back is so risky.
prereading.label: AFH 18-7 to 18-8

warmup: It is a hot afternoon, you are heavy, and the wind is gusty and across the runway. What three things will be different about this takeoff compared to a cool, calm morning?

key_terms.def: Speeding up from a stop until there is enough lift to fly [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].
The moment the wings lift the airplane off the surface, usually after you rotate the nose up [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].
Starts when you leave the surface in a climb attitude; ends at a safe maneuvering altitude or en route climb [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].
Gentle back-elevator pressure that raises the nosewheel slightly to the lift-off attitude [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
Best angle of climb speed: most altitude for a given distance over the ground [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Best rate of climb speed: most altitude in the least time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Better performance very close to the surface, up to about one wingspan high, because induced drag drops [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
The airplane's tendency on the ground to turn its nose into the wind [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].
Small bounces while drifting sideways in a crosswind; puts big side loads on the landing gear [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].
Stopping the takeoff while still on the runway: power to idle, brake, keep directional control [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

body.p: A takeoff is one smooth maneuver, but we learn it in three parts: takeoff roll, lift-off, and initial climb [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

Configuration means how the airplane is set up: flaps, power, trim and (if it has one) landing gear. Your POH/AFM gives the exact settings and speeds for your airplane. If the handbook and your POH disagree, the POH wins [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

bullets: Before taxiing onto the runway: all run-up and before-takeoff checklist items done; engine instruments normal; controls full, free and correct [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].
Takeoff: full takeoff power [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]; flaps and trim set as the POH says [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].
After a positive rate of climb: retract flaps and landing gear (if equipped) [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
Keep takeoff power until at least 500 feet above the surrounding terrain or obstacles [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
At a safe maneuvering altitude: set climb power and trim off the pressure [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

callout.text: Flaps and gear down cost climb. Lowering the gear or flaps reduces both excess thrust and excess power, so max climb angle and rate both get worse [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].

check.q: When do you retract the flaps after a normal takeoff?
check.a: Once a positive rate of climb is established (or as your POH says) [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

body.p: Before you go to the airplane, use the POH performance charts to see if you can take off and climb safely for today's conditions [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. The big inputs are pressure altitude and temperature (density altitude), weight, wind, and runway slope and surface [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

head: Factor
Effect on takeoff
Source
rows: Less engine and propeller performance, longer takeoff roll, worse climb
Higher true airspeed needed at lift-off (same indicated), and less thrust
About 5% higher takeoff speed and at least 21% longer takeoff distance
Longer ground roll (anything not hard and smooth)

body.p: Example: the POH says 1,000 feet of ground roll with no wind. With a tailwind of about 10% of your lift-off speed, plan on about 1,210 feet (21% more) [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]].

Why take off into the wind? A headwind gives you some airspeed before you even move, and you reach flying speed at a lower groundspeed, so the roll is shorter and easier on the gear [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]. Taking off with a tailwind is sometimes needed, but first check the POH says it is allowed and that you have the performance and runway [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].
Taking off from an intersection? You must check that the runway left from that point (and its declared distances) still covers what you need [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10]].

callout.text: Climb pitch will be lower when you are heavy or when density altitude limits power [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. Climb performance drops as altitude goes up [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].

body.p: Gusty wind? Stay on the ground a little longer to get extra speed, then rotate smoothly. A sudden lull at normal lift-off speed can mean loss of control or a stall [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

check.q: Name the four main things you must account for when predicting takeoff distance.
check.a: Pressure altitude and temperature (density altitude), gross weight, wind, and runway slope and condition [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

head: Speed
Gives you
Use it when
rows: Most altitude for the distance flown over the ground [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]
Clearing obstacles like trees or power lines off a short field [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]]
Most altitude in the shortest time [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]
Normal takeoff and climb; target speed for this Task

body.p: VX is usually a bit slower than VY. Your POH gives the actual numbers [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. In some airplanes, being just 5 knots off can cost a lot of climb, so fly the speed precisely [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Both speeds change with altitude and come together at the absolute ceiling [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].

callout.text: X = eXtra steep (angle, distance). Y = Yes, fastest up (rate, time).

check.q: You need to climb over tall trees at the end of a short runway. VX or VY?
check.a: VX, the best angle of climb, gives the most altitude over the shortest distance [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]].

chunks.title: Find the wind, set the controls

body.p: At a towered airport, ATC gives you the wind. Check the wind indicators anyway, even when someone reports the wind on CTAF, because that report may not be accurate [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]].

bullets: Wind cone / wind sock: the big end points into the wind [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]]. A sock also shows speed and gusts: it stands out straighter in strong wind and swings back and forth in gusts [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]].
Wind tee: the big end (cross bar) points into the wind [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]].
Tetrahedron: shows landing direction only. Don't use it for wind direction [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]].
No indicator? Use smoke from houses or factories, dust, brush fires, wind farms, or the patterns on nearby water [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

body.p: While taxiing and lining up, hold the controls for the wind. Quartering headwind: up aileron on the upwind wing (yoke into the wind), elevator neutral. Quartering tailwind: down aileron on the upwind wing (yoke away from the wind), elevator down [[24:56|AFH 2-19]], [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].
In a nosewheel airplane, hold the elevator neutral for headwinds [[24:57|AFH 2-20]]. On the takeoff roll, start with full aileron into any crosswind [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

check.q: Wind is a left quartering headwind. Where do you hold the ailerons and elevator while taxiing?
check.a: Left aileron up (yoke turned left, into the wind) and elevator neutral [[24:56|AFH 2-19]], [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: normal takeoff and climb

bullets: 1. Complete the before-takeoff checklist. Prepared checklists should be used before takeoff and after takeoff [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

2. Brief yourself: what you will do if the engine fails, including which way to turn toward landing areas given departure path, altitude, wind and terrain [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Pick the point on the runway where you must be airborne or you abort [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
3. Clear the area: make sure the approach and takeoff paths are clear of other aircraft [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].
4. Radio: at a towered airport, get a takeoff clearance before taxiing onto the runway. At a nontowered airport, announce your intentions on CTAF [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].
5. Line up on the centerline. Check heading indicator matches the runway heading before adding power [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. Pick reference points far down the runway [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].
6. Feet on the rudder part of the pedals, not the brakes. Release brakes and add throttle smoothly and continuously to takeoff power [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].
7. Check the engine instruments for any malfunction during the roll [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].
8. Keep straight with rudder (expect left pull from torque and P-factor); aileron into any crosswind; don't steer with brakes [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].
9. When the controls are effective, apply gentle back pressure to raise the nosewheel slightly. Hold that attitude until the airplane lifts off. Don't force it up [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
10. After lift-off: wings level, coordinated, hold the pitch that lets the airplane accelerate to VY [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
11. Positive rate of climb: flaps and gear (if equipped) up [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
12. Hold VY with small pitch changes on the horizon, then glance at the airspeed. Don't chase the needle [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
13. Track the extended centerline using two points lined up ahead [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].
14. Keep takeoff power to at least 500 feet above terrain or obstacles; at a safe maneuvering altitude set climb power and trim [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
15. Follow any noise abatement procedure for that airport [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

head: ACS skill
Standard
rows: Rotate and lift off; accelerate to VY
Manufacturer's recommended speed or VY, +10/-5 knots (ACS PA.IV.A.S11)
Maintain it, with proper wind-drift correction, through takeoff and climb (ACS PA.IV.A.S14)

body.p: Noise abatement: find each airport's procedures in the Chart Supplement, local publications, or from the tower. Signs at the hold position may remind you. If unsure, ask the tower [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

callout.text: Practice: say each step out loud on every takeoff. Have your instructor show you the lift-off and VY climb pitch so you memorize how they look [[24:136|AFH 6-4]]. Before your first solo, expect the airplane to lift off sooner and climb faster with only you aboard [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

check.q: What tolerance does the ACS give for your climb airspeed?
check.a: VY (or the manufacturer's recommended speed) +10/-5 knots (ACS PA.IV.A.S11 and S13).

bullets: Start of roll: full aileron into the wind. This keeps the upwind wing from rising [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].
Rudder keeps you straight. The airplane wants to weathervane into the wind, so you usually need downwind rudder [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].
As speed builds, ease off the aileron just enough to keep the wings level, but keep some in all the way [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].
Lift-off: it's fine if the downwind wheel lifts first. That is better than side-skipping [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].
Strong crosswind: hold the wheels on a little longer, then make a smooth but definite lift-off [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].
Once climbing: turn the nose into the wind (crab), level the wings, and stay over the extended centerline [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

body.p: The wind can change a lot within a few hundred feet of the ground, so check your ground track often and adjust the crab [[24:140|AFH 6-8]]. Expect a bit less performance in the roll because deflected ailerons and rudder add drag [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

Know your limit. Airplanes are tested for 90-degree crosswinds up to 0.2 VSO, and the demonstrated crosswind is placarded in airplanes certificated after May 3, 1962. Use a crosswind component chart and don't fly in wind beyond what the airplane can handle [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].

callout.text: Side-skipping (small bounces while drifting) puts severe side loads on the landing gear and can break it [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].

check.q: Wind from the right. Which way is the yoke turned at the start of the roll?
check.a: Fully to the right, into the wind [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

body.p: Windshear is a sudden, big change in wind speed or direction over a small area. Low-level windshear is the worst because you are close to the ground. Look for it with fronts, thunderstorms, temperature inversions and strong winds aloft (greater than 25 knots) [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
Taking off into a microburst: first a headwind (better performance), then downdrafts, then a growing tailwind (worse performance). It can push you into the ground [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

bullets: Microburst: downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30-90 knots; lasts about 5-15 minutes [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
Clues: heavy rain shaft at the surface with virga at cloud base, or a ring of blowing dust [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
Tailwind: needs a higher groundspeed to reach lift-off speed [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]. Only take off downwind if the POH allows it and you have the runway [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].

body.p: In studied takeoff accidents the climb looked normal at first, then a growing tailwind cut airspeed [[28:266|AWH 22-11]] and the pilot lowered the nose to get it back, giving away climb [[28:267|AWH 22-12]]. The AWH says to hold or raise pitch attitude and accept a lower airspeed, and that only 5 to 15 seconds may be available to react [[28:268|AWH 22-13]] [[28:269|AWH 22-14]]. On the runway, the only sign may be slower-than-normal airspeed buildup, and gusts can hide it [[28:270|AWH 22-15]]. These studies appear to involve large, crew-flown airplanes; your exact technique comes from the POH/AFM and your CFI.

Wake turbulence: wingtip vortices start when an aircraft lifts off [[1:361|PHAK 14-27]]. They are strongest when the aircraft is heavy, slow and clean [[1:361|PHAK 14-27]]. Taking off right behind a large airplane risks loss of control [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Note its rotation point, rotate before it, climb above its path until you turn clear [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go
Wait at least 2 minutes before takeoff [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
Worst case: vortices can sit on the runway [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]

callout.text: Tower may say "CAUTION - WAKE TURBULENCE," but with or without a warning, avoiding the wake is your job [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

check.q: A jet just did a touch-and-go on your runway with a light quartering tailwind. How long should you wait?

chunks.title: Plan for the bad day: abort and engine failure

body.p: Reasons to reject a takeoff: engine problem, poor acceleration, runway incursion, or traffic conflict [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

bullets: Before takeoff, pick a point on the runway where you must be airborne. Not flying by then? Abort right away [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
Runway needed to go and then stop: add the POH takeoff and landing ground roll distances for a good estimate [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
To reject: throttle to idle, maximum braking, keep directional control. For a fire: mixture idle cutoff and magnetos off. Always follow the POH emergency procedure [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

body.p: Engine fails after lift-off: you have only a few seconds. First, fly the airplane. At climb pitch with no power you are at or near a stall, so lower the nose right away and coordinate the rudder. Glide to a landing area, preferably straight ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

Straight ahead or a slight turn is usually the safest choice [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. Turning back (the "impossible turn") risks an accelerated stall and a downwind landing. In the FAA example, an engine failure at 300 feet AGL with a standard-rate turn back leaves the airplane 1,016 feet below the runway [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. A turn back at low altitude is an unacceptable risk for student pilots [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

callout.text: Stalls and spins near the ground: a spin needs a stall plus yaw. P-factor, torque, poor rudder use and windshear all cause yaw [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Power-on stalls are practiced so you recognize an accidental stall on takeoff or climb [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Flying at VY needs a quick response if the engine quits, to prevent a stall [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

body.p: CFIT (flying a good airplane into the ground) is often linked to high density altitude, mountainous terrain, low ceilings or visibility, and night [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. Know your climb performance against the terrain and obstacles off the end of the runway.

check.q: Engine quits at 200 feet AGL in a VY climb. What is your first action?
check.a: Lower the nose immediately to prevent a stall, coordinate with rudder, and glide to a landing area, preferably straight ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

chunks.title: Eyes outside: traffic, runway incursions, distractions

body.p: Collisions: before taxiing onto the runway, scan the approach area for landing traffic [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. Departing aircraft should always watch for arrivals from the opposite direction [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]]. At a nontowered airport, monitor CTAF from startup, during taxi and after departure [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.2]].

In the climb the nose blocks your view. Lowering the pitch a little helps you see traffic ahead [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]. Stay over the extended centerline so you don't drift into traffic from a parallel runway [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

CTAF example call (AIM): "Strawn traffic, Queen Air Seven One Five Five Bravo departing runway two six. Departing the pattern to the (direction), climbing to (altitude) Strawn." Say the airport name at the start and end, and say the runway number, not "active runway" [[33:210|AIM 4-1-9]] [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]].

Runway incursions: about 65 percent are caused by pilots [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. To avoid the wrong runway: carry a current airport diagram, set the heading bug to the runway heading, and do a last check that heading and runway match before adding power [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. At a towered airport, never enter a runway without an instruction to cross, take off, or line up and wait [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].

Distractions: many accidents start with a small problem, like a gauge reading wrong, that pulls the pilot's attention away from flying [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Do checklists early [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]] and while stopped [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]], so you have time for traffic and ATC on the roll and climb. If overloaded: stop, think, slow down, prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

callout.text: On the takeoff roll and climb: fly first (pitch, wings level, centerline), then look for traffic, then talk.

check.q: What is the last check before you add power on the runway?
check.a: Confirm the heading indicator matches the runway heading so you are on the right runway [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

head: Normal takeoff errors [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]
Crosswind takeoff errors [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]
rows: Not clearing the area before taxiing onto the runway
Not clearing the area before taxiing onto the runway
Abrupt throttle; not checking engine instruments after power
Less than full aileron into the wind at the start
Not expecting, or overcorrecting, the left turning tendency
Using aileron mechanically instead of watching your position on the runway
Wrong lift-off attitude; over-controlling elevator; no trim
Narrow scan, letting a wing (usually the left) drop after lift-off
Not enough rudder to stay parallel to the centerline
Not holding VY; chasing the airspeed indicator
Too much aileron late in the roll: steep bank at lift-off; poor drift correction after lift-off

body.p: Forcing the airplane off with too much back pressure can make it settle back or stall. Letting the nose drop after lift-off can also make it settle back [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

Ground effect fools you: the airplane may seem able to fly below the recommended speed [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. As it climbs out of ground effect, drag goes up and it tends to pitch up [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. At high density altitude, high temperature or max weight it may lift off but be unable to climb out of ground effect [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

check.q: Why is 'chasing the airspeed indicator' a problem?
check.a: Airspeed lags pitch changes. Set pitch on the horizon, hold it, then glance at the airspeed [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

scenario.title: Hot, gusty, and a jet ahead
scenario.setup: Summer afternoon at a nontowered airport. You and two friends are near max weight. Runway 26 is paved; runway 33 is shorter grass. The wind sock shows wind from about 300 degrees, gusty. A business jet just did a touch-and-go on runway 26. Far to the west you see a heavy rain shaft with a ring of blowing dust under it. Your friends are chatting and asking about the view as you taxi out.

questions.q: Which runway, and what do you check first?
questions.a: Run the POH numbers for density altitude, weight and wind. Grass adds ground roll [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]], and heavy plus hot means a longer roll and weaker climb [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Pick the runway that meets those numbers with margin, even if it means more crosswind within your limits.

questions.q: The jet just did a touch-and-go. What now?
questions.a: Wait at least 2 minutes; vortices settle on the runway, especially with a light quartering tailwind [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

questions.q: What about the rain shaft and dust ring?
questions.a: Those are microburst clues [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. A microburst can bring 30-90 knot headwind losses. A microburst lasts about 5-15 minutes [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]: wait for it to pass well clear, or don't go.

questions.q: Passengers keep talking during taxi. How do you handle it?
questions.a: Brief them before engine start that you need quiet during taxi, takeoff and climb. Distractions pull your attention off flying [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]; do checklists while stopped [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

questions.q: What's your plan if the takeoff goes wrong?
questions.a: Pick an abort point on the runway; not airborne by then, idle and brake [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. If the engine fails after lift-off: nose down, glide straight ahead or slightly to the side; no turn back [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

questions.q: Before rolling, what last checks prevent a collision or wrong-runway departure?
questions.a: Announce on CTAF, scan final (both directions) for traffic [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]], and confirm heading matches the runway before adding power [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

skills.do: Complete the before-takeoff and after-takeoff checklists.
skills.practice: Use the written checklist every flight. You can do the items, then use the checklist to verify nothing was missed [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

skills.do: Make the right radio calls: takeoff clearance at a towered field, CTAF announcements at a nontowered field.
skills.practice: Write your departure call on a kneeboard and say it aloud before flying [[33:210|AIM 4-1-9]].

skills.do: Confirm you are on the assigned/correct runway.
skills.practice: Set the heading bug to the runway heading and check it on every lineup [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

skills.do: Tell the examiner the wind direction, with or without a wind sock.
skills.practice: On every flight, find the wind from the sock and from smoke, dust or water [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

skills.do: Hold the controls correctly for the wind during taxi and takeoff.
skills.practice: Say the control position out loud each time you turn on a taxiway [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].

skills.do: Clear the area, taxi onto the runway, and line up on the centerline.
skills.practice: Look both ways down final, then line up and pick a far reference point [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

skills.do: Add throttle smoothly to takeoff power and check the engine and flight instruments before rotating.
skills.practice: Advance the throttle smoothly and continuously, then scan the engine gauges and airspeed every takeoff [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].

skills.do: Rotate and lift off at the recommended speed, then accelerate to VY.
skills.practice: Memorize the lift-off and VY pitch picture shown by your instructor [[24:136|AFH 6-4]].

skills.do: Hold the recommended speed or VY +10/-5 knots (ACS PA.IV.A.S11).
skills.practice: Set pitch on the horizon, hold, cross-check airspeed, trim [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

skills.do: Configure flaps, gear, power and trim per the POH.
skills.practice: Retract flaps only after a positive rate of climb; call it out [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

skills.do: Keep VY +10/-5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude (ACS PA.IV.A.S13).
skills.practice: Keep takeoff power to at least 500 feet above terrain or obstacles [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

skills.do: Stay on the centerline on the roll and on the extended centerline in the climb, correcting for drift.
skills.practice: Use two points lined up ahead of the runway as a tracking reference [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

skills.do: Follow noise abatement procedures where they exist.
skills.practice: Look them up in the Chart Supplement for each airport you fly from [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

quiz.q: A headwind equal to 10% of takeoff speed changes takeoff distance by about:
options: 10% shorter
21% shorter
19% shorter
50% shorter
quiz.why: A 10% headwind cuts takeoff distance about 19%; a 10% tailwind adds about 21% [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]].

quiz.q: VY is the speed that gives:
options: The most altitude for a given distance
The lowest stall speed
The most altitude in the least time
The best glide
quiz.why: VY gives the greatest gain in altitude per unit of time; VX gives the most per distance [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

quiz.q: At the start of a crosswind takeoff roll you should hold:
options: Neutral aileron
Full aileron into the wind
Aileron away from the wind
Full forward elevator
quiz.why: Apply full aileron into the wind as the roll begins [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

quiz.q: What does the ACS require for climb airspeed in this Task?
options: VY +10/-5 knots
VY ±10 knots
VX ±5 knots
VY +5/-10 knots
quiz.why: Maintain the manufacturer's recommended speed or VY, +10/-5 knots (ACS PA.IV.A.S11).

quiz.q: The engine quits during the initial climb. The first thing to do is:
options: Turn back to the runway
Lower the nose to prevent a stall
Restart the engine
Call ATC
quiz.why: At climb pitch with no power you are near a stall: lower the nose and keep coordinated first [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

quiz.q: Departing behind a larger airplane on the same runway, you should:
options: Rotate past its rotation point
Use full flaps
Stay low under its path
Rotate before its rotation point and climb above its path
quiz.why: Note its rotation point, rotate before it, and climb above its climb path [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

quiz.q: Taking off in strong, gusty wind, you should:
options: Lift off at the lowest possible speed
Use extra flaps
Get an extra margin of speed before lift-off
Rotate early to get out of the gusts
quiz.why: Stay on the ground a bit longer for extra speed so a lull doesn't cause loss of control or a stall [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

quiz.q: Which runway condition makes the takeoff roll longer?
options: Upslope
Hard, dry pavement
Downslope
Strong headwind
quiz.why: An upsloping runway slows acceleration and lengthens the ground run [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

quiz.q: Per the Aviation Weather Handbook, what pitch response helps after an inadvertent windshear encounter just after lift-off?
options: Hold or increase pitch attitude and accept lower airspeed
Lower the nose to regain normal climb airspeed
Reduce power and level off
Hold pitch for VX regardless of altitude loss
quiz.why: Lowering the nose to regain airspeed wastes performance; hold or raise pitch and accept reduced airspeed [[28:267|AWH 22-12]] [[28:268|AWH 22-13]]. Use the POH/AFM and CFI for your airplane's technique.

takeaways: Check POH performance before every takeoff: density altitude, weight, wind and runway all matter [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].
Smooth power, rudder for centerline, gentle rotation, then hold the VY pitch.
ACS: VY (or recommended speed) +10/-5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude.
Crosswind: full aileron into the wind to start, less as you speed up, then crab once airborne.
Pick your abort point and engine-failure plan before you roll; after lift-off, nose down and land mostly straight ahead.
Clear final, confirm the runway heading, and keep eyes outside.
cfi_notes: Students often hold too much back pressure right after lift-off and pitch up abruptly; demonstrate the lift-off and VY attitudes [[24:136|AFH 6-4]].
Students tend to fixate on pitch or airspeed and let a wing (usually the left) drop after lift-off [[24:137|AFH 6-5]] [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].
Teach control 'feel': the student should sense resistance, not move controls through wide ranges [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].
Brief the solo difference: lighter airplane lifts off earlier, climbs faster, controls feel more sensitive [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].
If there's no crosswind on checkride day, the examiner will test crosswind knowledge orally (ACS note).
Examiners often ask: abort point, engine-failure plan, why not turn back, VX vs VY, wake avoidance on departure.
Have students verbalize clearing ("clear left, right") to build the habit [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]].
gaps: Exact speeds (rotation, VX, VY), flap settings, power settings and max demonstrated crosswind are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM.
No resource gives a number for 'safe maneuvering altitude'; AFH only recommends takeoff power to at least 500 ft above terrain/obstacles.

AC 00-54 (Pilot Windshear Guide), cited by the PHAK, was cancelled by the FAA in 2022; this lesson uses the Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28B) instead. AWH 22-10 to 22-18 covers microburst effects, warning signs and the general principle of holding pitch attitude and accepting lower airspeed, but its encounter studies appear to involve large, crew-flown airplanes (crew coordination, stick shakers, aft body contact) and it gives no step-by-step windshear escape procedure for small airplanes. Get the airplane-specific technique from the POH/AFM and your CFI.
Task file has no S10 element (numbering jumps S9 to S11); lesson follows the file.
Airport-specific noise abatement procedures come from the Chart Supplement, which is not in the resources.

activities.title: Normal takeoff, step by step
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Line up on the centerline and check the heading matches the runway
Release the brakes and smoothly add full power
Check the engine instruments during the roll
Gentle back pressure to raise the nosewheel
After lift-off, hold the pitch that lets you speed up to VY
Positive rate of climb: flaps up
At a safe maneuvering altitude: set climb power and trim

activities.title: Crosswind takeoff: what do you do?
activities.intro: Tap a moment in the takeoff, then what you do.

pairs.r: Ease off aileron to keep wings level, but keep some in
Downwind wheel may lift first, and that's OK
Keep the wheels on a bit longer, then a definite lift-off
Turn the nose into the wind (crab) and level the wings

activities.title: True or false: when the takeoff goes wrong

cards.s: If you are not airborne at your planned abort point, stop the takeoff right away.
cards.why: Yes. Pick the point before takeoff, and if you are not flying by then, discontinue the takeoff at once [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

cards.s: A jet's wingtip vortices start at the beginning of its takeoff roll.
cards.why: No. Vortices come from lift, so they start when the aircraft leaves the ground, at its rotation point [[1:361|PHAK 14-27]].

cards.s: Adding the POH takeoff and landing ground rolls gives a good estimate of the runway you need to speed up and then stop.
cards.why: Yes. The AFH says those two distances added together are a good estimate [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

cards.s: After a jet's touch-and-go, waiting 1 minute is enough before you take off.
cards.why: No. Wait at least 2 minutes. Vortices can settle along the runway, especially in light quartering wind [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

cards.s: A standard-rate turn back to the runway from 300 feet AGL is a safe plan for a student pilot.
cards.why: No. In the FAA example that turn leaves the airplane 1,016 feet below the runway [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. A low turn back is an unacceptable risk for student pilots [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

cards.s: If the engine quits while you hold climb pitch, the airplane is at or near a stall.
cards.why: Yes. That is why you lower the nose right away and keep coordinated [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

final_quiz.q: You depart a high-elevation airport on a hot afternoon. Compared with a cool day at sea level, what changes at lift-off?
options: Lower indicated airspeed at lift-off, so a shorter roll
Higher indicated airspeed at lift-off, but the same true airspeed
Nothing at lift-off; only the climb is weaker
Same indicated airspeed, but a higher true airspeed and a longer roll
final_quiz.why: You lift off at the same indicated airspeed, but thin air means a higher true airspeed, and the engine makes less thrust. So the roll is longer [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]], and the climb is weaker too [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

final_quiz.q: The POH shows a 1,400-foot ground roll with no wind. Today the headwind is about 10% of your lift-off speed. About how long will the roll be?
options: About 1,130 feet
About 1,260 feet
About 1,690 feet
About 700 feet
final_quiz.why: A headwind of 10% of takeoff speed cuts takeoff distance about 19%: 1,400 x 0.81 = about 1,130 feet [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]. About 1,690 feet is what a 10% tailwind would give (21% longer).

final_quiz.q: With only you aboard, the POH shows a takeoff distance of 1,200 feet. You add a friend and bags, and the airplane is now 10% heavier. What should you expect?
options: About 1,260 feet, since takeoff speed goes up 5%
About 1,320 feet, a 10% increase
At least about 1,450 feet
About 1,200 feet, since weight only affects the climb
final_quiz.why: A 10% weight increase raises takeoff speed about 5% and adds at least 21% to takeoff distance: 1,200 x 1.21 = about 1,450 feet [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]. Use the POH chart for your real weight.

final_quiz.q: Your POH lists VX as 62 knots and VY as 74 knots. On a normal takeoff on the checkride, which climb speed range keeps you within standards?
options: 57 to 72 knots
69 to 79 knots
64 to 84 knots
69 to 84 knots
final_quiz.why: A normal climb uses VY, the speed for the most altitude in the least time [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. The ACS allows VY +10/-5 knots (PA.IV.A.S11): 74 + 10 = 84 and 74 - 5 = 69.

final_quiz.q: You taxi to the runway with the wind coming from your left rear (a quartering tailwind). How do you hold the yoke?
options: Turned left, elevator neutral
Turned right and pushed forward
Turned right and held back
Turned left and held back
final_quiz.why: For a quartering tailwind, hold the upwind (left) aileron down and the elevator down [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. That means the yoke turned away from the wind and pushed forward, so the wind can't get under the wing and tail and nose the airplane over.

final_quiz.q: The wind is from the left. You started the takeoff roll with full left aileron. As speed builds, the aileron feels firmer. What now?
options: Keep full left aileron all the way to lift-off
Center the yoke, since the crosswind no longer matters at speed
Ease off just enough to keep the wings level, but keep some left aileron in
Switch to right aileron to raise the left wing
final_quiz.why: As the ailerons get more effective, use just enough aileron to keep the wings level, and keep some in through the whole roll [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]. Too much aileron late in the roll gives a steep bank at lift-off [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

final_quiz.q: You are ready to depart runway 26 at Strawn, a nontowered airport. Which radio call is best?
options: Strawn traffic, Cessna 1234X departing the active, any traffic in the area please advise.
Cessna 1234X departing runway 26, heading north.
Strawn traffic, Cessna 1234X taking off now, Strawn.
Strawn traffic, Cessna 1234X departing runway 26, departing the pattern to the north, Strawn.
final_quiz.why: Say the airport name at the start and end, and use the runway number, not "active runway." "Traffic in the area, please advise" should never be used [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]]. The AIM's departure example follows this same pattern [[33:210|AIM 4-1-9]].

final_quiz.q: A large twin just flew a low approach over your runway and climbed away. In which wind is its wake most likely to still be lying along the runway when you are ready to go?
options: A strong, steady wind from straight ahead
A light wind from behind you, at an angle
A strong, gusty wind from ahead and to the left
A 20-knot wind from ahead and to the right
final_quiz.why: Near the ground, vortices drift with the wind. A light quartering tailwind is the worst case: the wake can sit along the runway and extended centerline [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go, wait at least 2 minutes [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

final_quiz.q: You take off and fly into a microburst you didn't see. What do you notice first?
options: Airspeed and climb get better from a growing headwind
A strong downdraft pushes you down right away
A growing tailwind cuts your airspeed right away
The airplane rolls hard toward the rain shaft
final_quiz.why: First comes a headwind that improves performance, then downdrafts, then a quickly growing tailwind that can push you into the ground [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. The early good climb is a trap.

final_quiz.q: Before takeoff you picked taxiway C, halfway down the runway, as the point where you must be flying. You reach it still on the ground, speeding up slowly. What do you do?
options: Keep going, since half the runway is still left
Add carburetor heat and continue the takeoff
Pull back hard to force the airplane into the air
Throttle to idle, brake, and keep straight
final_quiz.why: Not airborne at your planned point? Discontinue the takeoff right away: power to idle, maximum braking, and keep directional control [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Forcing it off too slow can make it settle back or stall [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

final_quiz.q: Your engine quits at 400 feet AGL right after takeoff. You have lowered the nose. Where do you plan to land?
options: Back on the departure runway, using a standard-rate turn
Back on the runway, using a steep turn, since pavement is safest
Anywhere you can reach after circling once to lose height
A field straight ahead or slightly to one side
final_quiz.why: Straight ahead or a slight turn is usually the lowest-risk choice. In the FAA example, a standard-rate turn back from 300 feet AGL leaves the airplane 1,016 feet below the runway [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. A low turn back is an unacceptable risk for student pilots [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

final_quiz.q: Hot day, max weight. The airplane lifts off a little below the recommended speed and floats a few feet up, but it won't climb. What is happening?
options: The airspeed indicator reads too high, so you are slower than you think
Ground effect cut the drag near the surface; higher up, drag rises and it can't climb
The wings are making too much lift, so the airplane is held in a level float
The climb pitch is too low, so pulling back harder will fix it
final_quiz.why: Near the ground, induced drag drops, so the airplane may seem able to fly below the recommended speed. At high density altitude, high temperature or max weight it may lift off but be unable to climb out of ground effect [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. Lift off at the recommended speed.

final_quiz.q: In the climb, your airspeed is 5 knots below VY. What is the best way to fix it?
options: Watch the airspeed indicator and keep moving the nose until it reads VY
Add back pressure to raise the nose
Lower the nose slightly against the horizon, hold it, then glance at the airspeed
Reduce power so the airplane climbs less steeply
final_quiz.why: Use attitude flying: change pitch on the horizon, hold it, then check airspeed. The airspeed takes a moment to change, so watching only the needle leads to chasing it [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
